report:
## Conclusion

The claim that ibuprofen worsens COVID-19 is **not supported by the weight of evidence**. It originated from a March 2020 tweet by France's health minister and a *Lancet Respiratory Medicine* correspondence proposing a biologically plausible but unproven mechanism: NSAIDs might upregulate ACE2 receptors (the SARS-CoV-2 entry point), theoretically facilitating infection ([thelancet.com](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lanrhe/article/PIIS2665-9913(21)00144-2/fulltext)). This triggered widespread public alarm and shifting national guidance.

However, major regulatory and health bodies quickly reviewed the actual clinical evidence and found no support for the claim. The FDA stated it was "not aware of scientific evidence connecting the use of NSAIDs, like ibuprofen, with worsening COVID-19 symptoms" ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-alerts-and-statements/fda-advises-patients-use-non-steroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs-nsaids-covid-19)), and the WHO similarly walked back its initial caution, concluding there was no evidence ibuprofen worsens the condition ([cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/health/ibuprofen-covid-19-novel-coronavirus-1.5501496)).

Subsequent controlled studies reinforced this. A large multicenter cohort of 78,674 hospitalized COVID-19 patients across England, Scotland, and Wales found NSAID use was **not** associated with worse mortality, ICU admission, or need for ventilation; some studies even showed a reduced risk with NSAID use ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9107579/)). A review of the ACE2-linkage hypothesis also noted it was based on limited correspondence, not robust clinical trials, and the theoretical mechanism was never confirmed clinically ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7486973/)).

**Bottom line:** The mechanistic hypothesis was reasonable to investigate, but empirical clinical evidence—including large cohort studies—does not support that ibuprofen worsens COVID-19 infection.
